hints: Focus on what makes beryllium the odd one out in Group 2, its tiny size and very high charge density.
Check burning in oxygen, reaction with dilute acid, and nitrate decomposition, as Be and Mg actually behave the same in those three cases.
Consider which chloride is covalent enough to be hydrolysed by water to release acidic fumes, and which one simply dissolves.
walkthrough:
**Recall the anomalous position of beryllium**

Beryllium is the first element in Group 2 and is very small with a highly polarising $\text{Be}^{2+}$ ion. This makes some of its compounds more covalent, but many basic Group 2 reactions are still the same for Be and Mg.

Key idea:
$$\text{similar group chemistry, except where high charge density causes hydrolysis}$$

**Test the first three properties, they are the same**

Both metals burn in oxygen to form oxides, both react with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to give sulfates plus hydrogen, and both nitrates decompose on heating in the same way.

$$2\text{M} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MO}$$
$$\text{M} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{MSO}_4 + \text{H}_2$$
$$\text{M}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow \text{MO} + 2\text{NO}_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$$

**Spot the real difference in chloride hydrolysis**

$\text{BeCl}_2$ is essentially covalent and is readily hydrolysed by water to give acidic $\text{HCl}$ fumes. $\text{MgCl}_2$ is more typically ionic and just dissolves to give a slightly acidic solution, with no fumes.

$$\text{BeCl}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Be}(\text{OH})_2 + 2\text{HCl}$$

options.A: Incorrect. Both Be and Mg burn when heated in air to form the white oxide, MO. Magnesium famously burns with a brilliant white flame, so the claim that Mg does not react is false.
options.B: Incorrect. Both metals react with dilute aqueous $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to form $\text{MSO}_4$ and $\text{H}_2$. Magnesium actually reacts more vigorously than beryllium, which has a protective oxide layer, so the claim that Mg does not react is false.
options.C: Incorrect. Both $\text{Be}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ and $\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ decompose on heating to give the oxide, $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$. This is the standard Group 2 nitrate decomposition, so there is no difference here.
options.D: Correct. This is the true difference. $\text{BeCl}_2$ hydrolyses in water to release fumes of $\text{HCl}$ because the tiny $\text{Be}^{2+}$ ion strongly polarises water molecules. $\text{MgCl}_2$ does not fume like this, it simply dissolves.
